verses.text: “Do you think this to be your right, or do you say, ‘My righteousness is more than God’s,’
That you ask, ‘What advantage will it be to you? What profit shall I have, more than if I had sinned?’
I will answer you, and your companions with you.
Look to the heavens, and see. See the skies, which are higher than you.
If you have sinned, what effect do you have against him? If your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him?
If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?
Your wickedness may hurt a man as you are, and your righteousness may profit a son of man.
“By reason of the multitude of oppressions they cry out. They cry for help by reason of the arm of the mighty.
But no one says, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
who teaches us more than the animals of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of the sky?’
There they cry, but no one gives answer, because of the pride of evil men.
Surely God will not hear an empty cry, neither will the Almighty regard it.
How much less when you say you don’t see him. The cause is before him, and you wait for him!
But now, because he has not visited in his anger, neither does he greatly regard arrogance.
Therefore Job opens his mouth with empty talk, and he multiplies words without knowledge.”

footnotes.content: Elihu steps forward with another word. This fourth friend is younger, has listened long, and now his turn comes. There's something both tender and presumptuous in a young man believing he's found what three elders have missed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu claims Job has set his righteousness above God's—a hard charge, and not quite fair to what Job said. Yet there's a grain of truth: Job does demand God answer, as if justice lies with him to measure. We too can drift into believing God owes us explanation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job has asked what profit righteousness brings if suffering comes anyway. It's the ancient cry: why obey if the wicked prosper too? Elihu hears in Job a transactional faith—goodness as a bargain with God. But faith that demands return is not quite faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu promises to answer Job and his friends together. He's gathering them under one rebuke—all have failed to see what he will now make plain. The confidence of youth is on full display; he means well, but wisdom seldom announces itself so loudly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Look to the heavens, and see." It's the oldest argument—when words fail, point upward. The sky stretches higher than any human sorrow, declaring God's greatness. Elihu is right: in the face of such immensity, our grievances shrink, and so does our demand that God justify Himself to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you sin, does it wound God? If you rebel, do your acts diminish Him? No. Elihu cuts at the root of Job's complaint: you assume your suffering proves God cares for you personally, but perhaps He cares for something far larger. Your pain may not be about you at all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nor does your righteousness profit Him. You cannot give God what He lacks or strengthen His hand. This is true—and humbling. We work righteousness not because God needs it, but because He has made us to thrive in it. Our obedience is for us, not for Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your wickedness touches others—a man like yourself; your righteousness lifts the son of man. The circle of our deeds is small and human-scaled. We affect each other, not the throne of heaven. It's freeing and terrifying: we are responsible to one another, not to justify ourselves to God's ledger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu shifts. He speaks now of the oppressed who cry out under mighty hands, crushed by power they cannot match. They weep—but who do they call upon? The question hangs. In suffering, the heart often looks first to the arm that hurt it, not to God's arm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?" A stunning phrase. Not songs of day—anyone sings then. But songs in the night, when darkness presses close and the bones ache. Elihu asks: do the suffering ask God for a song, or do they only curse the darkness?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God teaches us more than the beasts, makes us wiser than the birds. We alone can turn our face to the Maker and ask. The animals suffer; they do not question. A human being who suffers yet refuses to ask God for wisdom may be choosing the way of the beast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cry but receive no answer—not because God is deaf, but because their cry is hollow. "Because of the pride of evil men." The proud do not truly ask; they demand. Their cry carries no humility, no real seeking. Pride closes the ears more surely than distance does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God will not hear an empty cry." Elihu is clear: not all crying reaches heaven. The cry must carry something—repentance, faith, or at least honest seeking. An empty cry is all wind and no root. Job, in his pain, must ask himself: is my complaint rooted in truth, or in the pain that clouds my sight?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You say you do not see Him—and then you wait for Him? There's a contradiction Elihu presses. If God is truly hidden from you, why wait? If He is real but you refuse to see, then waiting is self-deception. Faith is not waiting for what you've already decided does not see you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God has not visited in anger, yet Job speaks as if condemned. Perhaps, Elihu suggests, the silence is mercy, not rejection. And arrogance—the refusal to bend, the insistence that you alone are right—such things God does not greatly regard because they are not worthy of regard. They are small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu's final blow: Job opens his mouth with empty talk and multiplies words without knowledge. Readers today hear an echo of our own age—how readily we fill silence with our own noise, how often we speak without listening. Perhaps the hardest wisdom is knowing when to hold still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
